title: Classifying Product Catalogs with Multimodal Embeddings
subtitle: Results of the Q4 experiments
author: Rodrigo
notes: Thank you all for joining. Over the last quarter we ran a focused set of experiments to see whether combining product photos with titles can fix the worst misclassifications in our catalog. In the next ten minutes I will walk through why the current text-only model struggles, how our multimodal prototype works, what the held-out results look like, and what it takes to ship this safely.

bullets: Image + text embeddings beat text-only classification by 8 accuracy points (89% vs. 81%)
Largest gains appear on 1-3 word titles where text alone is ambiguous
Recommendation: run a 10% shadow deployment before replacing the production classifier
slides.notes: Here is the headline up front so we stay anchored on the decision. Adding frozen image embeddings to our existing title classifier raised held-out accuracy from 81% to 89%. Even more encouraging, the biggest jump happens on short one-to-three-word listings where sellers give us almost no text to work with. Because inference latency stays under 40 milliseconds, our recommendation today is to approve a low-risk shadow rollout on 10% of live traffic.

We will cover three short parts today. First, the catalog problem and why short listings fail today; second, the architecture of our frozen-backbone prototype; and third, the benchmark numbers, error analysis, and rollout plan.

slides.notes: Our production classifier only looks at the title, which works fine when a seller writes a detailed nine-word description, but falls apart on mobile listings with titles like 'Leather strap' or 'Classic mug'. Those sparse listings drive nearly half of our manual category corrections. By bringing in the primary product image, the model can see the object directly instead of guessing from two ambiguous words.

slides.notes: A key design choice here was keeping both upstream encoders frozen. Rather than fine-tuning a large multimodal transformer—which would require GPUs in serving and weeks of retraining—we precompute normalized image and text vectors and train a simple regularized linear layer on top. That keeps training under ten minutes on a single machine and lets us reuse cached embeddings across experiments.

slides.title: Handling Missing Product Photos

code.title: Bug: zero-vector leaks into head
Fix: route to text-only fallback

slides.notes: One subtle bug we caught during shadow testing was how missing photos were handled. Originally, passing an all-zero image vector shifted the multimodal classifier's decision boundary and cost six points of accuracy on photo-less listings. Routing those requests directly to the calibrated text-only head eliminates the distortion cleanly.

slides.title: Results & Trade-offs
slides.subtitle: How much better is it, and where does it still fail?
slides.notes: Now let's look closely at the evaluation results on our 20,000-product held-out split.

slides.title: Headline Held-Out Performance

callout.label: accuracy gain over text-only baseline (89.1% vs. 81.1%)
bullets: Evaluated on 20k stratified held-out listings with seller-level split
Macro-F1 improves by +9.4 pts, showing gains aren't limited to head categories
CPU p95 inference latency stays at 38 ms (budget: 50 ms)

slides.notes: Headline result first: overall accuracy jumps from 81.1% to 89.1% on a seller-grouped test split, which ensures the model isn't memorizing a single merchant's phrasing. Just as important, macro-F1 climbs by 9.4 points, confirming that medium and smaller categories benefit too. Latency stays at 38 milliseconds on CPU, comfortably inside our 50-millisecond serving SLA.

slides.title: Single-Modality vs. Multimodal Benchmark
slides.notes: To make sure the photo was truly adding orthogonal signal, we benchmarked four variants side by side. Neither modality wins alone: image-only reaches 76.4%, and even adding seller descriptions only gets text to 84.3%. Combining title and photo beats every single-modality baseline by nearly five points because visual cues resolve noun ambiguity while text resolves fine-grained product attributes.

slides.title: Accuracy by Title Length
slides.notes: Breaking accuracy down by title length shows exactly where that eight-point average comes from. On short one-to-three-word listings, accuracy leaps by 18 percentage points—from 68% to 86%—because the photo supplies the context missing from the title. Once a title exceeds nine words, text already carries most of the signal, though the image still catches occasional seller typos.

grid.title: Packaged & boxed goods
grid.text: Close-up boxes look visually similar; weight title tokens higher when confidence drops.

grid.title: Image embedding cost
grid.text: Compute image vector once at upload time and cache in the feature store.

slides.notes: Before we ship anything, let's be candid about the four failure modes we observed in error analysis. About 11% of listings lack a valid photo at creation time, so the service falls back automatically to the text head. Visually generic packaging and rare categories under 50 samples remain weaker, which is why we want a shadow run before turning on auto-assignment.

slides.notes: Rather than flipping 100% of traffic on day one, we propose a staged rollout over the next month. Offline validation is complete. If you approve today, we will deploy in shadow mode for two weeks to verify real-world photo quality and latency under production load, then graduate to seller suggestions before full cutover.

bullets: Multimodal embeddings deliver +8 pts accuracy (+18 pts on short titles) within our 50 ms SLA
Architecture stays simple: frozen encoders with a lightweight, fast-to-retrain linear head
Decision needed: approve 2-week 10% shadow deployment starting Monday
slides.notes: To wrap up: adding the product photo solves our single biggest blind spot—short seller titles—while keeping serving complexity low and latency under budget. All risks around missing images and packaged goods are bounded by a fallback path. What I need from you today is a green light to start the two-week 10% shadow test on Monday.
